text.p: The International Brotherhood of Teamsters on Thursday rejected what United Parcel Service of America Inc. had described as its final offer, but the union sought further talks ahead of a midnight strike deadline.

Ken Hall, co-chairman of the Teamsters' National Negotiating Committee, said the UPS offer failed to address key issues, including an end to sub-contracting, more full-time jobs and health and safety issues.

"UPS claims to have made a final offer," Hall said. "The fact is the last offer that UPS has put on the table does not address all the serious issues and the serious proposals that we have put on the table," he said, adding decent wages and pensions to that list.

Hall, speaking from Washington, said the union was ready to go back to the table and hold further negotiations. Asked if a strike could still be avoided, he expressed confidence: "Absolutely, if the company comes to the table and negotiates seriously we can reach agreement before midnight."

UPS, the nation's largest package distribution company, said its "last, best and final" contract offer would increase pay for both full- and part-time workers by $1.50 to $2.50 per hour over five years. It said it would also guarantee that no UPS driver is replaced or eliminated through subcontracting.
The company's current contract with the Teamsters expires at midnight EDT. UPS has said it cannot promise it will be able to continue to complete deliveries after Thursday.

The company also said the new offer proposes a restructuring of UPS pension benefits. It said the offer, made Wednesday, includes a wage and benefits package that would keep UPS Teamsters the highest-paid workers in the industry.

The company said it would agree to provide 10,000 opportunities for part-time employees to move into full-time jobs over the life of the agreement. It would also create 1,000 new full-time jobs from part-time jobs.

The company said the pension restructuring it has proposed would increase monthly benefits for full- and part-time employees by an average of 50 percent. Retirees would be covered under new pension plans created outside the Teamsters' multi-employer pension system, it said.
"We recognise that it is difficult for the union leadership to accept this new pension plan," UPS spokesperson Ken Sternad said in a statement.

"It became clear to us that the union was intent on drawing these negotiations out indefinitely because of the pension issue. However, we believe UPS dollars should directly benefit UPS employees, not support the Teamsters' pension funds," Sternad said.

It said its pension plan would provide up to $3,500 a month in retirement pay for full-time employees and includes early retirement options beginning at 25 years of service. It said current Teamsters pension plans can pay less than $1,000 a month after 25 years of employment.
UPS said its offer to the union is "a fair and generous offer that addresses all key points raised by the union during negotiations."
The Teamsters represent about two-thirds of the company's domestic payroll, including delivery truck drivers, tractor- trailer drivers and package facility workers.
